newsitem.title: USA: Paccar bids $543 million for Dutch DAF Trucks.
newsitem.headline: Paccar bids $543 million for Dutch DAF Trucks.

text.p: Paccar Inc. plans to buy Dutch-based DAF Trucks NV for $543 million in a friendly deal that would give it a foothold in continental Europe, the two companies said Monday.
"This offer demonstrates PACCAR's commitment to being a global leader in the heavy-duty commercial truck market," Paccar Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Charles Pigott said in a statement.

Industry analysts said the deal would strengthen Paccar's position in Europe against such global rivals as Freightliner, a unit of Daimler-Benz; Renault, maker of Mack trucks; and a joint venture of Volvo and General Motors Corp.
"This will patch a hole for them in Europe," said analyst Paul Latta of Ragen MacKenzie. "It puts Paccar on a more even footing with the global heavy-duty truck manufacturers.

The offer drew a positive initial response from DAF's biggest shareholder, the Dutch government, which acquired a 39 percent equity stake after leading the move to create a new truck-building company from the ashes of its bankrupt predecessor, DAF NV.
But Wall Street took a defensive view, and Paccar's stock fell 62.5 cents to $50.50 in Nasdaq trading.
The deal, which is subject to shareholder approval, is expected to close by the end of the year, Paccar said.
Paccar, which markets vehicles largely under the Peterbilt and Kenworth names, is the world's No. 3 maker of heavy-duty trucks. But it has little presence in Europe outside its Foden unit in Britain.
DAF has about 9 percent of the West European market, concentrated in Britain, the Netherlands and Belgium.

"The company is profitable right now and it is interested in expanding and growing its market share in all of these different countries," Paccar Vice Chairman Mike Tembreull said in a conference call with analysts.
"We see this as another Kenworth or Peterbilt which will help Paccar achieve its profit goals in the future," he said.

Unlike Paccar, which mainly assembles trucks with components from other manufacturers, DAF makes its own engines and other key parts. Tembreull said that in addition to cost savings from the combination of the two companies, Paccar would consider expanding DAF's profitable parts business to new markets.
He said the deal would immediately be additive to Paccar's earnings, although he declined to provide details.
Paccar, with output last year of 54,000 vehicles, made a net profit of $253 million on sales of $4.6 billion in 1995.
DAF Trucks, which produced more than 16,600 vehicles at its Eindhoven plant in 1995, made a net profit of $96 million on sales of $1.69 billion.
The old DAF NV had been a far larger company, with annual output of 26,000 trucks and 22,000 vans following its 1987 takeover of the British Leyland commercial vehicles business.
Mounting losses and crippling debt forced DAF NV to file for bankruptcy in February 1993, but it was relaunched later that month with the British operations sold off.
DAF Trucks said Paccar's offer had the support of DAF's two main management organs.

"Together we will have greater innovative power and technological possibilities," said DAF Trucks Chairman Cor Baan. He said Paccar planned to run DAF Trucks as an independent unit, retaining the DAF and Leyland DAF marques.
A spokesman for Dutch Minister of Economic Affairs Hans Wijers said the government welcomed Paccar's approach but would need to examine it carefully before making a final decision.
Paccar has four plants in the United States, where it has a 21 percent share of the market, and it has manufacturing facilities in Australia, Mexico and the United Kingdom.
